cards.title: Post-Purchase Upsell Mechanics and Benchmarks
cards.summary: Post-purchase one-click offers carry near-zero friction, commonly hit 25–40% take rates, and can add 10–15% revenue per visit.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add post-purchase offers and how to set expectations for their impact on AOV.
steps: Place offers after payment capture so the customer has already committed; with correct setup it is effectively one click and instantly charges the saved card.
Treat this as near-zero friction and consider it standard: the source says 'I would always have this.'
Expect high take rates — the presenter reports people running 35–40% take rates, though that is an observed example, not a guarantee.
Compute revenue per visit (RPV) as post-purchase revenue divided by post-purchase funnel visits, or as average upsell value times conversion rate.
Target roughly 10–15% RPV; at a $200 AOV that is about $20 extra per order.
You can sell almost anything here, so this stage rewards A/B testing more than any other.
caveats: All figures depend on correct implementation; the presenter flags the 'if implemented correctly' caveat explicitly.
Take-rate and AOV-lift numbers are examples from other brands, not promised results.
Stringing multiple post-purchase offers is effective for the advertiser but annoying to consumers — a deliberate trade-off.

cards.title: String Post-Purchase Offers: Anchor High, Then Down-Sell
cards.summary: Sequence post-purchase offers from a high anchor downward so later price points feel cheap, the opposite of how most brands do it.
cards.use_when: Building the order and number of post-purchase offers in a funnel.
steps: Lead with a high-value upsell, roughly $50–60, to set the price anchor.
If declined, down-sell into the $20–30 range.
If the high offer is taken, move them to another upsell slightly lower at $30–40, then a second down-sell.
If the first down-sell is declined, flow them to down-sell number two.
Expect declining take rates at each step — for example 25% on the first offer and 10% on the second — but each additional take compounds onto AOV.
The payoff reported: supplement and CPG brands using stacked post-purchase offers increased AOV by 50–60%, which let them be far more aggressive on acquisition and spend double on Facebook.
caveats: Most brands invert this by leading with the cheapest offer; the source says anchoring at $20 makes every later high-value upsell look expensive.
Stacked offers are consumer-annoying; the presenter openly dislikes receiving them.
AOV lift percentages are case examples, not benchmarks to plan against.

cards.title: Cross-Sell vs Upsell: Definitions and Fit
cards.summary: A cross-sell is a complementary different product alongside the purchase; an upsell is more of the same product, usually with a discount.
cards.use_when: Choosing which in-cart offer type fits your catalog and buyer.
steps: Define cross-sell: a different but complementary product — buying a t-shirt and being offered matching socks or shorts.
Note that cross-sells fit multi-SKU brands best because you are selling into other products.
Define upsell: more of the same — buying a one-month supply and being offered a three-month supply with a discount.
Apply the relevant mechanics: bundles and cross-category offers for multi-SKU catalogs; product repositioning and larger pack sizes for single-hero-SKU catalogs.
caveats: The source admits it went most of the way through before defining the distinction, so treat the terms as planning vocabulary rather than rigid categories.

cards.title: Five Rules for In-Cart Upsells and Cross-Sells
cards.summary: One offer per cart slot, relevance over price, high-margin SKUs, legible offers, and measure gross margin lift not AOV lift.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing in-cart upsell and cross-sell offers.
steps: One offer per slot in the drawer cart: three offers cause decision fatigue that lowers take rates more than it helps.
Focus on relevancy over price: a good price means nothing if the product is not contextual to what is in the cart.
Choose high-margin SKUs; avoid upselling something that only adds a few dollars of gross profit when a relevant high-margin item could sit there instead.

Keep the offer easy to understand — you have roughly two to three seconds for it to be legible, which usually means a flat discount on the added item, unlike front-end offers where complexity can increase.
Measure success by gross margin lift, not AOV lift, or you will over-prioritize low-margin SKUs that may have higher AOV.
caveats: The flat-discount simplicity rule applies to cart cross-sells and upsells, not to front-end offers, where the source argues for more complexity.

cards.title: Four Questions to Select the Right Offer
cards.summary: Gross margin floor, AOV distribution, single vs multi-SKU, and repeat behavior determine which offer constructs are viable.
cards.use_when: Starting offer design or diagnosing why an offer is not working.
steps: Ask what the gross margin floor is, so you can model whether an offer improves profitability or just erodes margin for no net benefit.

Examine the AOV distribution: with two peaks, split the offer across those thresholds to move customers up; with one peak (e.g. supplements with a 30-day supply), focus on moving the core audience to a larger size.

Determine whether you have a single hero SKU or multiple SKs. Single-SKU brands should lean on product repositioning as the highest lever, then gift with purchase, and be disciplined with discounting. Multi-SKU brands can use native bundles, cross-category upsells, and threshold mechanics that unlock products.

Assess buyer repeat behavior: with repeats, you can build subscriptions and time-limited offer cycles into the front end; with little repeat, focus on sustaining gross margin on the first order, since that is where most gross margin comes from.
caveats: The source stresses this is a starting framework, not a predictor: of 100 possible offers, about 10 are good, and nobody can say which will win until it is tested in market.

cards.title: Offers Are Not Discounts: The Five Mechanics
cards.summary: The offer is the construct; the discount is one mechanic inside it, usually the worst one to lead with.
cards.use_when: When a team defaults to a percentage-off promotion as its offer strategy.
steps: Replace 'our offer this period is 25% off' with a designed construct: the five offer mechanics are product repositioning, bundles, gift with purchase, tiered thresholds, and disciplined straight discounting.
Lead with mechanics other than discount where possible, since discounting is usually the worst thing to lead with.

Recognize the offer as one of the most important acquisition levers — test front-end acquisition offers in separate funnels with dedicated landing pages, because the offer changes profit on first purchase and what retention looks like.
caveats: The source is explicit that discounting is not banned — it is one mechanic, and 'disciplined' straight discounting is part of the five.

cards.title: Six In-Cart Mechanics Beyond Price Cuts
cards.summary: Samples, threshold unlocks, shipping-margin capture and post-purchase adds give margin lift without discounting headroom.
cards.use_when: Looking for in-cart and checkout mechanisms that add contribution margin without a blanket promo.
steps: Add samples or a complimentary product as a threshold unlock once the customer hits a spend level.
Use the in-cart threshold bar at the top of the cart ('add one more product and you'll get a particular price') as the placement for these unlock mechanics.

Monetize shipping: shipping is close to 100% margin, you almost never actually refund it, and if you do, the carrier normally pays — a simple way to add $1–$2 of contribution margin or gross profit to every order with no overhead.
Use post-purchase for one-click adds, and treat post-purchase as the place where almost anything can be sold.
caveats: Shipping as pure margin depends on your carrier terms and refund policy; verify before relying on it.

cards.title: New vs Returning Customer Offers Must Differ
cards.summary: New-customer offers optimize first-purchase economics; repeat offers deepen cohorts, so the same offer should not run to both.
cards.use_when: Setting the promo calendar for acquisition versus retention audiences.
steps: For new customers, optimize for first purchase economics and getting the customer in the door.
For repeat customers, design offers that deepen cohorts by locking buyers into a sustainable purchase period.
Therefore the two offers should look meaningfully different, despite the common habit of running one offer at both groups.
caveats: The source presents this as a fundamental mismatch, and it is also listed as failure mode number three.

cards.title: AOV Distribution vs Mean AOV for Setting Thresholds
cards.summary: Set free-shipping and threshold offers from the AOV distribution curve, not the mean, which is a top-cited failure mode.
cards.use_when: Choosing tiered threshold levels for offers.
steps: Plot the AOV distribution of your customers rather than relying on mean AOV.
If two peaks exist, split the offer across those thresholds and use them to move customers up.
If there is a single peak, focus on moving the core audience into spending more — for example from a 30-day supply to a 90-day supply in supplements.
caveats: The source estimates that 80% or more of practitioners set thresholds off mean AOV, which results in a wrongly configured offer — treat that as the presenter's estimate, not measured data.

cards.title: Iterate and Rotate Offers Over Time
cards.summary: Offers should not stay static; survey existing customers and split test new offers on dedicated landing pages while the live offer runs.
cards.use_when: Planning ongoing offer testing after you have a customer base.
steps: Once you have a large enough existing customer base, survey those customers as much as possible to iterate on the offer.
Expect that offers typically do not stay static; even big CPG brands that keep an offer for 6–12 months are usually split testing different offers on dedicated landing pages and funnels in parallel.
Rotate the winning test offer into the main funnel, because finding a better offer is one of the most valuable front-end wins once creative and other elements are dialed in.
Run dedicated funnel and landing page tests for front-end acquisition offers to measure profit on first purchase and downstream retention.
caveats: This assumes creative and the rest of the funnel are already dialed in; otherwise offer tests are confounded.
Requires enough traffic and a large enough customer base to test and survey meaningfully.

cards.title: Seven Ways Offers Fail
cards.summary: Common failure modes: blank discount as offer, miscomputed gross margin, one offer for new and returning, thresholds off the mean, wrong gift, endless promo calendar, and treating Q1 as seasonal.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing offer program for structural problems.
steps: 1. Stop defaulting to a blank percentage discount and calling it an offer — the offer is more than a discount.

2. Calculate gross margin correctly: include shipping and fulfillment impact (which can improve in bundles as units per transaction rise), and understand how margin affects efficiency targets like ROAS, or you will discount too hard to ever hit efficiency thresholds.
3. Segment new versus returning customers, since these are different mechanics.
4. Set thresholds from the distribution curve rather than mean AOV.

5. Choose gift-with-purchase gifts with care — a gift customers don't care about won't move take rates, and a gift that isn't high margin enough won't change the economics of the bundle. Rank the math before adding the gift.
6. Avoid a continuous 25-week promo calendar that rotates percentage discounts across categories and calls it offer rotation; it is unsustainable and locks you in forever.

7. Treat Q1 as an offer problem, not a seasonal dip. Rotate contextually relevant offers into Q1, and use Q1's suppressed conversion rates and market sentiment as one of the best windows to test offers.
caveats: These are the presenter's observed failure modes, framed as diagnostics rather than proven causal findings.

cards.title: Discount Planning Needs an Efficiency Target Model
cards.summary: Model how a discount changes contribution profit and the ROAS you must hit, instead of planning discounts in isolation.
cards.use_when: Approving a discount depth or planning a promo calendar against paid media efficiency.
steps: Model the two sides together: how contribution profit and average order value change as discount depth changes, and what efficiency (e.g. ROAS) you must hit on paid platforms for the offer to work.
Without the curve, you will set discounts without knowing the required efficiency, and efficiency will never reach the discount threshold needed to maintain margin.

Use the source's position that the offer is a primary acquisition lever: changing the offer alters profit on first purchase and influences retention, so it belongs in the acquisition plan, not only in the promo calendar.
caveats: The source references a discount/efficiency calculator behind a link in its description; verify availability and current interface before relying on it.

cards.title: Single-SKU vs Multi-SKU Offer Strategy
cards.summary: Single-hero-SKU brands lead with product repositioning and are disciplined with discounts; multi-SKU brands can use bundles, cross-category upsells and threshold unlocks.
cards.use_when: Choosing offer mechanics based on catalog structure.
steps: For a single hero SKU, use product repositioning as the highest lever, then gift with purchase, and keep straight discounting disciplined.
For multiple SKs, build native bundles, run cross-category upsells alongside bundles, and add threshold mechanics that unlock different products.
Combine this with repeat-behavior analysis: subscription and purchase-cycle offers fit repeat buyers, while one-off categories should protect first-order gross margin.
caveats: The source presents this as its four-question selection framework's third question; it is a decision aid, not a validated rule.

A cross-ell is a different complimentary product alongside what you're already buying. So, an example is that if you buy a t-shirt, we go and offer matching socks or matching shorts. This is best for multisq brands because you're selling into other products. But an upsell is just selling more of the same. So, if you're buying the one month supply, we're going to offer you a 3mon supply with some kind of discount. Now, an additional metric that you can track here for post-purchase offers is what's called RPV, which is revenue per visit. You take post purchase revenue captured and you divide by post purchase funnel visits. You can also calculate this by average upsell value times by conversion rate. Now, the idea here is this is just telling you how many dollars extra are you making out of every person that goes into the funnel as a function of the post-purchase upsell. Now, a good benchmark that you want to aim for is 10 to 15%. If you don't currently have post-purchase upselles, well, the crazy revelation if you made it this far in the video is that you can add 10 to 15% to your average order value overnight just by adding post-purchase upsells if they are done well. You want to always anchor high and then downell below it. And most brands end up inverting this where they lead with the cheapest offer because they think it'll convert better.
